metaDescription: Medify MA-14, MA-25, MA-35, MA-40, MA-50 and MA-112 compared by CADR, honest room size, fan speeds and filter upkeep so you pick the model that fits.
expertTake: The MA-40 is the model most homes should buy, because its CADR of 406 serves a large bedroom or living room at moderate fan speeds. The MA-14 is the compact choice for a small room and the MA-112 is a commercial-scale machine for very large spaces. If you want an app, a particle display or automatic fan control, this family offers none of them and you should look elsewhere.
introParagraphs: Some purifier brands sell sensors, apps and glowing rings. Others sell airflow and a filter, and let the numbers do the talking. This family belongs to the second group: plain metal-cased machines with a few fan speeds and a published clean air delivery rate.
That simplicity is a strength when you know your room size and a weakness when you want automation. The comparison below translates the numbers into rooms so you can match model to space.

products.name: Medify MA-40 HEPA H13 air purifier, CADR 406
products.description:
The MA-40 is the sweet spot of the family. A CADR of 406 means that by the 2/3 rule it can serve a room of roughly 600 square feet at allergy-grade air changes, which is a large bedroom, a living room or a small open-plan space. The 1,793 square feet in an hour on the box is a single-air-change figure, so use the CADR to size the room instead.

It is a plain machine: three fan speeds, an H13 HEPA filter with a carbon layer and no sensor. The lowest setting is listed as nearly silent, but the top speed moves a lot of air and is clearly audible. The tradeoff for the simplicity is that you set the speed yourself, and the machine will not ramp up when you cook. Beyond the MA-35 it adds about 40 percent more airflow.

Ownership is a filter replaced on a schedule, typically within a year, and a wipe of the metal case. Place it with a few inches of clearance on all sides and keep it off thick carpet so the intake stays clear.
products.bestFor: Large bedrooms and living rooms that want strong airflow without electronics.
pros: CADR of 406 serves about 600 sq ft at allergy-grade changes
H13 HEPA with a carbon layer
Metal case with simple three-speed controls
Quiet on the lowest setting
cons: No sensor, app or auto mode

products.name: Medify MA-35 HEPA H13 air purifier, CADR 290
products.description:
The MA-35 is the bedroom workhorse. Its CADR of 290 supports a room of about 435 square feet by the 2/3 rule, which covers nearly any bedroom with margin to spare, so it can idle on a low setting and stay quiet through the night.

It shares the MA-40's H13 filter and plain three-speed control, in a slimmer body. The compromise is capacity: in a living room or open plan it would work at its top speed continuously, which defeats its quiet advantage. Against the MA-25 it moves roughly twice as much air for a modest step up in size and cost.

Upkeep follows the family pattern: replace the filter on schedule, wipe the case and keep the intake clear. Because it rarely needs a high setting in a bedroom, the filter tends to last toward the long end of its range.
products.bestFor: Bedrooms and home offices up to a large size.
pros: CADR of 290 gives a margin in a bedroom
Can idle on a low setting overnight
H13 HEPA filter with carbon
Slimmer body than the MA-40

products.name: Medify MA-14 HEPA H13 air purifier, CADR 120
products.description:
The MA-14 is the small member of the family, a tabletop machine with a CADR of 120. The 2/3 rule puts that at a room of about 180 square feet, which is a small bedroom, a nursery, a dorm or a home office.

Its value is in the compact body and low price tier, with the same H13 HEPA approach as the larger models. The limit is plain: in a room above about 200 square feet it will not turn the air over often enough for allergy-grade cleaning, however long it runs. It is also louder per unit of air than the large machines, because a small fan works harder.

Set it at table height with space around it, replace the filter on schedule and keep the vents clear of dust. It makes sense as a second machine for a desk or a child's room.
pros: Compact tabletop body
CADR of 120 suits about 180 sq ft
Same H13 filter approach as larger models
Lowest price tier in the family
cons: Too small for rooms above about 200 sq ft
Small fan is louder per unit of air

products.name: Medify MA-25 HEPA H13 air purifier, 825 sq ft
products.description:
The MA-25 steps up from the MA-14 with more airflow in a tabletop format, listed for 825 square feet in an hour. That figure is a one-change number, so a sensible bedroom target is about half of it.

It is a plain machine with three fan speeds, an H13 HEPA filter and a carbon layer for odors. A machine this small is easy to knock over on a crowded nightstand, so give it a flat, stable spot. Like the rest of the family, it has this limit: no auto mode and no sensor, so you choose a speed and live with it. Between the MA-14 and MA-35 it is the right size for a standard bedroom that does not need the larger body.

Vacuum dust from the vents occasionally and replace the filter on schedule. It runs on a standard 110 volt outlet and is easy to move between rooms.
products.bestFor: Standard bedrooms that want a tabletop footprint with more airflow than the MA-14.
pros: More airflow than the MA-14 in a tabletop body
H13 HEPA with a carbon layer
Easy to move between rooms
Simple three-speed controls
cons: Less headroom than the MA-35 in bigger bedrooms

products.name: Medify MA-50 V3.0 HEPA H13 air purifier, CADR 598
products.description:
The MA-50 V3.0 is for big rooms. A CADR of 598 supports roughly 900 square feet by the 2/3 rule, which is a large open living area, a basement or a bonus room. Four fan speeds give a little more control than the smaller models.

The filter is the same H13 HEPA concept with a carbon layer, scaled up in a larger cabinet. At that size the machine is a presence in the room, and the top speed is loud, so the sensible use is a medium setting for most of the day. Against the MA-40 it gives about 50 percent more airflow, and against the MA-112 it is far smaller and easier to place.

Give it clear floor space and plan for a larger filter replacement than the compact models need.
products.bestFor: Large open living areas and basements.
pros: CADR of 598 serves about 900 sq ft
Four fan speeds
H13 HEPA with a carbon layer
Strong airflow at moderate speeds
cons: Large and loud at the top speed
Larger filter costs more to replace

products.name: Medify MA-112 V3.0 dual HEPA H13 purifier, CADR 1009
products.description:
The MA-112 is a commercial-scale machine with a CADR of 1009 and dual HEPA H13 filters. By the 2/3 rule that supports around 1,500 square feet at allergy-grade changes, which is a whole open floor, a large classroom or a small office.

Two filters mean twice the filter area and twice the replacement cost, and the cabinet is the biggest in the lineup. It is overkill for a bedroom and noisy at the top speed, but it is the only model here that can actually serve a very large space. Against the MA-50 it moves about 70 percent more air.

Place it in a central position with open space around it. Because it is heavy, think about the route to its final spot before you unbox it, and give it a spot near an outlet so you do not need an extension cord, which is a poor idea for a machine that runs all day. For most homes, two smaller machines in two rooms are a better answer than one MA-112.
products.bestFor: Very large open spaces, classrooms and offices.
pros: CADR of 1009 for very large rooms
Dual H13 HEPA filters
Four fan speeds
Serves about 1,500 sq ft at allergy-grade changes
cons: Very large and loud on the top speed
Two filters double the replacement cost

buyingCriteria.criterion: Use CADR, not the one-hour figure
buyingCriteria.explanation: The MA-40 lists 1,793 square feet in an hour, but that is a single air change. Its CADR of 406 supports about 600 square feet at the 4 to 5 changes used for allergy-grade cleaning, via the 2/3 rule. Always size from CADR: the MA-14's 120 serves about 180 square feet, the MA-35's 290 about 435 and the MA-50's 598 about 900.

A machine that is slightly larger than the room can run at a low, quiet speed and still hit the target air changes. A machine that is just big enough must run at its top speed to keep up. For a 300 square foot bedroom the MA-35 gives that margin, while the MA-14 would be working hard.

These purifiers have three or four fan speeds and no sensor, app or auto mode. That means the machine will not ramp up when you cook or vacuum, so you must do it yourself. If you want automation, this family is the wrong tool, but if you want a simple, steady machine, it is a good fit.

H13 HEPA with carbon filters need replacing on a schedule, usually within a year, and larger models have larger and costlier filters. The MA-112's dual filters double the cost. Check genuine filter prices for your model before buying, and avoid off-brand filters that may not seal against the housing. Set a reminder when you install a new filter, because there is no indicator light on a plain machine to tell you when it is spent, and a filter that is overdue quietly stops doing its job.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Consider noise at the top speed
buyingCriteria.explanation: The lowest settings are close to silent, but the top speeds move a lot of air and are clearly audible. The MA-50 and MA-112 are loud at maximum. A larger machine on a medium setting is quieter than a small machine on high, so size matters for noise. A good habit is to run the machine at a higher speed for an hour when you vacuum, cook or dust, then drop it to a low setting for the rest of the day. That routine gives you the benefit of high airflow when particles are airborne and the quiet of a low setting when the room is calm.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Do not buy for a space it cannot serve
buyingCriteria.explanation: The MA-14 and MA-25 are tabletop machines that will not clean a large living room however long they run. The MA-112 is overkill for a bedroom. Match the model to the room, and for a big home consider two smaller units in two rooms instead of one giant one.

specDecoder.meaning: The clean air delivery rate in cubic feet per minute, measured at the highest speed. It is the best measure of how much clean air a machine produces.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MA-40's 406 and MA-112's 1009 are top-speed figures, and lower speeds deliver less.

specDecoder.meaning: The room area the machine can cycle once per hour. It is a single air change, not allergy-grade cleaning.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MA-50's 2,640 square feet in one hour supports about 900 square feet at proper changes.

specDecoder.meaning: A guide that the minimum CADR is about two thirds of the room's square footage, for 8 foot ceilings.
specDecoder.watchFor: Higher ceilings reduce effective coverage, so size up.

specDecoder.meaning: A high-efficiency filter grade that captures at least 99.95 percent of fine particles. True HEPA is 99.97 percent at 0.3 microns.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MA-112 uses two of them, which raises both capacity and replacement cost.

specDecoder.meaning: The area the machine can clean in 30 minutes, effectively two air changes per hour.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MA-40's 896 square feet in 30 minutes is a better guide than its hourly figure.

howWeEvaluated.title: CADR and room fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted each model's CADR into a room size using the 2/3 rule. The MA-14, MA-35, MA-40, MA-50 and MA-112 were then matched to rooms from about 180 to 1,500 square feet. Hourly coverage claims were discounted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Filter system
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the HEPA grade and carbon layer on each model. All use H13 HEPA, and the MA-112's dual filters earned credit for capacity. Replacement frequency was noted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls
howWeEvaluated.description: The family's manual speeds were compared with automated machines. They earned credit for simplicity and lost points for the lack of a sensor. No model scored for smart features.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and build
howWeEvaluated.description: Metal cases and the near-silent lowest setting were credited. Top-speed noise on the larger models was marked down. We used owner feedback patterns and listing details.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership cost
howWeEvaluated.description: Filter size, count and replacement cost were compared across the line. The compact models cost the least to maintain, and the MA-112 the most.

howToChoose.subheading: One Big Unit vs Two Small

cards.label: One large unit
cards.text: The MA-112 or MA-50 covers a big open space with one machine. It costs more to filter and is loud at the top speed.

cards.label: Two smaller units
cards.text: A MA-35 or MA-40 in each of two rooms often cleans more air where you live, with quieter running and lower filter costs.

howToChoose.note: Choose one big unit only for a single large open space, and two smaller ones for separate rooms.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A high CADR, an H13 HEPA filter, a carbon layer and enough margin to run at a medium speed. Smoke is the hardest particle to capture, so oversize the machine.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The MA-40 and MA-50 give strong CADR, and the MA-112 handles very large spaces. In a bedroom, the MA-35 gives a margin.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The room is large, you live with smoke or heavy allergens or you want margin to run quietly, which points to the MA-40 or MA-50.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The room is small, where the MA-14 or MA-25 does the job.

maintenance.why: The carbon layer saturates and the HEPA layer loads. Late replacement lowers airflow and lets odors return.
Dust collects on the grille. Keeping it clear protects airflow.
Dust builds up on the surface. A dry cloth is enough.
Furniture and curtains block flow. Leave a few inches around the unit.
A frayed cord is a hazard on a machine left running. Check where it meets the plug.

faq.q: Which Medify should I buy for a bedroom?
faq.a: The MA-35 gives a margin in most bedrooms thanks to a CADR of 290. For a small bedroom, the MA-25 or MA-14 is enough.

faq.q: Does Medify have an app or auto mode?
faq.a: No. These models use manual fan speeds with no sensor. If you want automation, choose a different brand.

faq.q: How do I size one for my room?
faq.a: Use CADR and the 2/3 rule: multiply the CADR by about 1.5 to get the room size in square feet at allergy-grade changes.

faq.q: How often do the filters need replacing?
faq.a: About every 6 to 12 months depending on use. Heavy smoke or pets shorten the interval.

faq.q: Is the MA-112 worth it for a home?
faq.a: Rarely. It suits very large open spaces, but two smaller units in two rooms are quieter and cheaper to filter for most homes.
The lowest settings are close to silent, but the top speeds are audible. A larger machine on a medium setting is quieter than a smaller one on high.
